standard.title: Addition and Subtraction Situations
standard.description: represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can quantify and compare collections using counting (AC9MFN03) and use part-part-whole reasoning to partition and combine collections to 10 (AC9MFN04). They have not yet represented joining and separating situations as mathematical relationships using materials or drawings.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification using physical and virtual materials, and use counting or subitising strategies to find results.

nodes.label: Representing additive situations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a practical addition or subtraction situation using materials or drawings, showing what is happening in the story.
nodes.minimum_width: Use materials or a drawing to represent one addition or subtraction story situation (e.g. objects joining a group, or objects leaving a group).
nodes.typical_width: Represent a range of practical addition and subtraction situations using materials or drawings; connect representations to oral story contexts; show the action (joining, separating) in the representation as well as the result.
wider: Represent additive situations from First Nations Australians' stories (e.g. 'Tiddalick the Greedy Frog') and leaf games from the Warlpiri Peoples of Yuendumu — describing the mathematical relationship
Compare addition and subtraction situations side-by-side, identifying what is the same (a change in quantity) and what is different (joining vs separating)

response_modes.reason: Students commonly represent only the final state (the answer), not the additive action. Encountering addition and subtraction situations through varied stories and contexts — particularly those requiring active role-play — makes the joining and separating actions visible in the representation. Varied contexts resolve the tendency to show just the endpoint.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to use counting or subitising on a representation to find a result — but if the representation shows only the final state (not the action), there is nothing for the strategy to operate on. Students who represent endpoint-only cannot use their representation to solve the problem or communicate the mathematical situation in node 3.
success_criteria: Student represents an addition or subtraction situation with materials or drawings that show both the starting state and the action (joining or separating)
Student can describe what their representation shows in relation to the story

nodes.label: Finding results using counting or subitising
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use counting or subitising to find the result of a represented addition or subtraction situation.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent an addition or subtraction situation and use counting to find and state the result.
nodes.typical_width: Use counting or subitising strategies to find results of addition and subtraction situations; record the result with a numeral; apply strategies across a range of practical story contexts including simple quantity comparisons.
wider: Role-play simple money transactions using $1 coins — representing the situation, counting coins to find the result, and connecting the count to the transaction context
Compare counting-on as a strategy (starting from the larger group) with counting-all — discussing which is more efficient for different quantity sizes

response_modes.reason: Reliable use of counting strategies requires fluency in one-to-one counting under the pressure of a story context. Students commonly lose track when objects are added to or removed from a group mid-count. Repeated practice across varied situations builds the procedural reliability needed.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to represent and solve quantification situations across varied context types — which depends on reliably applying a counting or subitising strategy. Students who lose track mid-count cannot solve varied situation types or connect mathematical representations to real-world contexts.
success_criteria: Student finds the result of an addition or subtraction situation using counting or subitising and records it with a numeral
Student selects an appropriate strategy (counting all, counting on, subitising) for the quantities involved

nodes.label: Representing quantification contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent and solve practical quantification situations (comparing, enough for a group, simple transactions) using materials and counting.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent and solve one quantification situation (e.g. 'do we have enough for everyone?') using materials and counting.
nodes.typical_width: Represent and solve practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification across a range of everyday contexts; connect mathematical representations to the real-world situation; use counting or subitising strategies to find results across all situation types.
wider: Represent and solve additive situations from First Nations Australians' instructive games (e.g. leaf games from Warlpiri Peoples) — connecting mathematical structure to cultural context
Create own story situations that involve addition or subtraction and represent them for a partner to solve
Investigate how the same additive structure (joining, separating, comparing) can appear in very different story contexts — connecting mathematical sameness across varied stories

response_modes.reason: Quantification situations (enough for a group, comparing, transactions) require students to identify the additive structure of a real-world problem, represent it, and solve it — integrating nodes 1 and 2 in a purposeful context. The integration of representation and strategy selection across varied situation types is the endpoint demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Varied practical contexts — money, sharing, group sufficiency, story problems — give advancing students rich opportunities to connect the same additive mathematical structure to very different real-world situations. This builds transferable mathematical reasoning beyond just computation.
success_criteria: Student correctly represents and solves an addition, subtraction or quantification situation using materials and counting or subitising
Student connects their mathematical representation to the real-world context (can explain what the materials or drawing shows)
